items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Hackers may have found a surprising new target: Your grocery store’s frozen food aisle
items.content_html:
Grocery stores across Europe faced an overnight cyberattack on Monday, affecting the refrigerated and freezer sections and leading to product losses.

The new wave of cyberattacks affected grocery stores in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, and Estonia, Reuters previously reported..The attacks took place overnight, raising the temperatures both freezer and refrigerator units to 122 degrees Fahrenheit resulting in widespread food spoilage and some units catching fire.

The attacks affected major retailers across the continent including stores owned by Ahold Delhaize, Colruyt, ICA and Coop.  IKEA—which also sells frozen food including its iconic meatballs—also confirmed to Fast Company that one location in Mons, Belgium has also been affected.

“Our teams are investigating to better understand the nature and scope of the incident and any potential impact on our operations. We are also carrying out precautionary checks across our markets,” an IKEA spokesperson told Fast Company.

Fast Company also reached out to Ahold Delhaize, Colruyt, ICA and IKEA for comment but did not receive a response by publication time.

Coop confirmed to Fast Company that around seven of 800 Sweden locations were affected by the attack, with issues ranging from complete refrigerator and freezer shutdowns to partially functioning equipment, and one instance of a system generating heat. According to Carlos Cancino, head of press relations at Coop Sweden, the affected locations are now fully operational again.

The incidents follow a similar cyberattack in France last month, which affected around 700 grocery stores with losses estimated at tens of millions of euros. The attacks, which also raised the freezer and refrigerator system’s temperature to around 122 degrees, caused loss of food and some fires.

“They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it—a warning that we must take seriously,” EU commissioner for agriculture, Christophe Hansen, told Reuters. “The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning.”

The widespread attacks have been possible due to technologies that allow for remote controlling in-store systems from freezers to surveillance cameras. Both attacks seem to have compromised internet-connected units using mostly temperature control technology from Danish engineering company Danfoss.

The attacks point to growing vulnerabilities in the food supply chain. Last year, United Natural Foods (UNFI) faced “unauthorized activity” on its IT systems, with grocery stores across the country experiencing disruptions as a result from the attacks.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] AI and women at work: 5 positives, 8 negatives
items.content_html:
The debate about AI and work often focuses on the jobs that will disappear, which tasks will be automated, and which skills and qualities will be valued in the future. Seldom do I read articles that analyze the impact of AI on exhaustion and pleasure at work. And those questions are usually asked about “workers” in general, as if the answers were the same for men and women. There are many reasons why they are not. Because women and men are concentrated in different occupations, perform different tasks within the same organizations, and are judged differently for the same work, artificial intelligence affects women’s work in very specific ways.

Is the overall effect positive or negative? It isn’t easy to say, so I made an old-fashioned list of pros and cons, the kind people draw up when deciding whether to change jobs or leave a relationship. I ended up with more negatives than positives: five reasons to be hopeful and eight reasons to worry.


On the hopeful side

1. Today’s job growth is happening mostly in women’s jobs, and they aren’t very much exposed to AI. In 2025, healthcare and social assistance accounted for almost all net job creation in the U.S.—about 405,000 jobs in healthcare and 308,000 in social assistance. If it weren’t for those two sectors, the U.S. would have lost jobs last year. The Bureau of Labor Statistics anticipates that this will continue to be the case in the coming decade because of population aging. We will need a lot of caregivers in the future, and large language models (LLMs) can’t take their place. That protects women’s employment, but it does little for their pay: Care work remains poorly compensated, and in the U.S. its growth also depends on public money that hinges on political choices. The coming midterm elections will say a lot about where things are heading.

2. AI could make “greedy jobs” less hostile to women. A big part of the pay gap is attributable to the unequal distribution of the highest-paying jobs. The so-called “greedy jobs” reward presenteeism and excessive workloads, which penalizes everyone who can’t give work all of their time. In law, finance, consulting, or medicine, value is tied to being the one person who knows the client or the case. If AI makes expertise portable, making a client’s or a case’s history immediately accessible to other colleagues, then it could reduce the premium on being irreplaceable. This is what digital records did to the pharmacy industry, which went from a male-dominated, unequal profession in 1970s America to an equal one. Of course, we’ll still need employers to decide to redesign those jobs, and that can never be guaranteed. 

3. Hurrah, some of the most tedious office chores are now being automated. Writing meeting minutes, taking notes, organizing schedules, drafting follow-up emails: Most of these “non-promotable tasks” are important but do nothing to advance the career of those who do them. And they fall predominantly on women’s shoulders. (That shouldn’t come as a surprise: They’re exactly like household chores.) The time spent on them could be spent on more visible tasks that can earn you a promotion. So AI tools that automate them are more than welcome! Likewise, there’s less paperwork in care jobs. Nurses and doctors are worn down by paperwork. Using AI tools can help them focus more on patients, which happens to be the part of the job they like best.

4. The barriers to entrepreneurship and to building with tech are lower now. Women who start companies have always had to do more with less. In the U.S., startups founded only by women still get roughly 2% of venture capital (and this share isn’t budging). AI makes it possible to start small and still go far. On your own, you can accomplish so much more with an army of “agents”! You can create a website with very little money, draft contracts, and answer customers. According to equity management platform Carta, the share of new startups with a single founder rose from about 24% in 2019 to 36% in the first half of 2025. AI-assisted coding also enables people to develop digital tools without knowing how to code, which is remarkable in a field where women are in the minority. 

5. Relational skills are gaining value. As AI takes over the codifiable part of cognitive work, the value of what it doesn’t do so well could go up: coordinating, caring, and exercising judgment in context. A lot of women have acquired these skills through decades of being expected to look after others and manage their emotions. If AI does raise the value of those skills, the market may have to pay more for them and stop seeing them as “naturally” feminine and therefore of little value. 

On the worrisome side

1. The most exposed white-collar jobs are disproportionately held by women. In rich countries, according to the International Labour Organization, 9.6% of women’s jobs fall into the highest category of exposure to generative AI, compared with 3.5% of men’s jobs. The reason is that women are concentrated in clerical jobs: assistants, secretaries, and payroll and data entry clerks. Not all these jobs will disappear. But we already have an idea of how they can change. Translation is a mostly female profession (around 7 in 10 translators and interpreters in the U.S. are women). A big share of translators have lost work to generative AI (and others have changed professions already). Many of those who still have work now spend their days editing machine output, for less money. 

2. The first rungs of the ladder are disappearing. For generations, junior administrative and clerical jobs were a route into employment, as well as upward mobility, for women without higher education. A secretary could become an office manager, then an executive assistant, then an operations manager. If AI eliminates most of these entry points, the career ladder gets cut at the bottom—and that’s bad news for women.

3. Women who use AI pay a competence penalty. In a study of more than 1,000 engineers reported by the Harvard Business Review, identical code was judged differently depending on who was known to have written it. Women who used AI saw their perceived competence drop by 13%, compared with 6% for men, and by 26% when the reviewers were men who did not use AI themselves. This is a digital version of the Matilda effect: When a woman uses the machine, the credit goes to the machine; when a man uses it, his judgment in choosing to use it is valued. Women are caught in a double bind: They are judged less competent if they use AI and less up to date if they don’t. 

4. Women are largely absent from one of today’s most lucrative industries. AI is already one of the best-paid segments of the market. According to LinkedIn, women accounted for only 26% of AI hires in 2025, compared with half of all hires in other sectors, and they hold only 13% of C-suite roles at AI companies. 

5. The tools are built mostly by men, and it shows. LLMs learn from data that reflects a world where men have long held the best jobs and earned the highest salaries. German researchers at the Technical University of Applied Sciences Würzburg-Schweinfurt asked chatbots for salary negotiation advice using profiles that were identical except for gender. Women were told to aim lower. In one case, the model suggested $280,000 for a woman and $400,000 for a man. Years earlier, Amazon had to drop an experimental recruiting tool after discovering it penalized CVs containing the word “women,” as in “women’s chess club captain.” The system had been trained on 10 years of applications, most of which came from men. In hiring, evaluation, and career advice, the same biases get repeated at scale.

6. New office chores replace the old ones. Someone still has to read the automated minutes, improve the AI-generated drafts, and catch the made-up figures and other hallucinations before they go out. AI slop takes time to process. I suspect a lot of this “cleanup” lands where office chores have always landed. If that’s right, some of the time saved by automating the old chores gets eaten by the new ones.

7. The jobs AI can’t do are the ones it watches most closely. Call centers and home care are good examples. In the U.S., 85% of home care workers are women, and since 2020, those paid through Medicaid have had to log every visit in an app that tracks them by GPS and checks their identity. Call center and retail workers know the same timed tasks and automated schedules. These women keep their jobs, but they lose more and more control over how they do them.

8. Deepfakes make visibility more dangerous for women. Nearly all deepfake videos online are pornographic, and 99% of the people targeted in them are women. Public life makes it worse: In the U.S. Congress, women were 70 times more likely than men to be targeted. Journalists, politicians, founders, and anyone whose career depends on being seen now face a risk men rarely do. Many women are likely to respond by stepping back—and who could blame them? After facing online abuse, 38% of women journalists surveyed by UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization) said they had lowered their public profile.

On balance

My list clearly has more negatives than positives, which in itself doesn’t mean much. Counting items doesn’t tell you how much each one weighs. Besides, the list is far from comprehensive. You may have other arguments on the credit or the debit side.

Still, having drawn up both columns, I would say the balance is negative for women’s work, at least for now. The main reason is a difference in timing. Most of the negatives are already happening: Women hold the most exposed jobs, the first rungs of the career ladder are disappearing, women who use AI are judged more harshly, they are a small minority in the sector where the money is, the tools carry biases, the jobs AI can’t do are increasingly monitored, and deepfakes make public visibility riskier.

Most of the positives, on the other hand, depend on conditions that haven’t yet been met: Greedy jobs will only loosen if firms deliberately redesign work, the time freed from office chores and paperwork can easily be swallowed by new tasks, and relational skills will only pay if employers finally choose to recognize them.

The balance could still shift, of course. What happens next will depend on choices made inside companies (about job design, evaluation, and hiring in AI) and on choices made at the ballot box (about how much public money goes to care).

items.content_html: Chinese AI company DeepSeek’s Harness team released an open-source coding-agent prototype on Oct. 31 that routes developer messages and software events into separate worker sessions rather than relying on a single prompt-and-response chat. DeepSeek says its internal system can reproduce and fix bugs reported in group chats, handle code reviews and help develop its Harness project. In DeepSeek’s internal tests in a simplified, synthetic environment, half of tasks finished within 12.4 minutes and 95% within 15.7 minutes. Remaining challenges include scaling the system beyond a single router and securing cloud agents that can access local files and credentials.

items.content_html: Google said its Project Suncatcher prototype satellite has returned its first AI-generated response from orbit. The satellite ran the Gemma 4 model on a data center-class Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) and transmitted a haiku during a ground-station pass over Svalbard, Norway. The satellite launched on Oct. 1, and Google described the response as an early milestone in research into operating AI computing hardware in space. The experiment tests whether the hardware can function in orbit; it is not a deployed computing service. Google’s next tests will examine performance under thermal stress and radiation exposure. The company says a successful trial could lead to two interconnected satellites in 2027.

items.title: [blog.talosintelligence.com] Cisco Talos urges Chrome controls to block VOLTA credential theft
items.content_html: Cisco Talos researchers recommend restricting which programs can launch Chrome in headless mode to block a credential-theft technique used by VOLTA, a Windows infostealer they analyzed. The malware steals credentials, account sessions and cryptocurrency wallet data, then builds a dossier that can help an operator identify valuable targets. Talos says it has not established whether VOLTA has been used in real-world attacks. Talos says VOLTA’s token theft relies in part on bypassing Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption by launching the browser in headless mode. It recommends that security teams set alerts for unapproved processes that do so. The malware can delete itself, and Talos observed no attacker-owned infrastructure. Researchers say the sample records what it harvested and whether its AI analysis succeeded in a timestamped debug file. Talos advises incident responders to preserve that file, revoke potentially stolen tokens and change passwords. Wallets whose seed phrases were stored in plaintext should be replaced.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Enterprise AI is waiting for its PageRank moment
items.content_html:
Let’s try a little thought experiment in technology-fiction: what would have happened if Larry Page and Sergey Brin’s PageRank, back in 1998, had failed to attract its first investors? Google didn’t invent the search engine: there were plenty of them before, from AltaVista, Excite, Lycos or others who were counting words on pages and selling their results page to the highest bidder, to catalog or portal concepts such as Yahoo! or AOL, that attempted to capture the users’ attention as much as they could to be able to serve them advertising, the more the better. Imagine if these concepts would have gone the distance, and deprived us of the web that resulted from Google’s easy and efficient way of searching … 

What did Larry Page and Sergey Brin realize? They adapted and extended the citation index (or its consequence, the citation impact), a system that they knew worked for academic literature (remember, these guys were graduate students working on their Ph.D., and thus reading academic papers like there was no tomorrow!), and moved it into a new context: the web. They realized there was an underused signal, relationships among pages, and used it to generate a metric, weighting links according to the importance of the pages providing them, that not only allowed them to index the web, but also to define attention as a social construct: a page is important when other pages link to it with a certain term. 

What’s today’s underused signal in corporate AI? 

As I’ve said several times, corporate AI is completely different from individual AI: companies don’t need just answers to questions, what they need is persistent memory and state, feedback learning loops, embedded cybersecurity, logs that can be tracked and not manipulated, etc. 

So far, companies are building these required scaffolding using twentieth-century tools such as Python, and AI agents are proving to be smart enough as to escape from these containments and do all sort of bad things — not because they are intrinsically evil (they cannot be), but because the goals and the guardrails are badly defined, or due to excessive permissions, prompt injection, or weak isolation. These companies are trying to define these properties by repeatedly assembling application by application, rather than supplied coherently by the platform. 

However, companies are repeatedly making all sorts of decisions about suppliers, customers, inventory, pricing, service, etc. Those decisions are constantly generating evidence of what works and what not, provided that the company is smart enough to capture them. What if we could evaluate AI by whether the company learns and improves, beyond the quality of individual outputs? What if AI optimization becomes more important than having access to bigger models? 

The competition moves from model capabilities to system performance 

A company does not just need a very powerful AI model: it needs an architecture that coordinates capabilities toward its goals. Researchers writing on Berkeley’s AI research blog explicitly describe the shift toward compound AI systems, where system design can offer better returns than further model scaling. 

Other experiments, such as FrugalGPT or DSPy are specific precedents for making model selection subordinate to results: FrugalGPT demonstrated that model cascades can match the strongest individual model with up to 98% lower cost on its evaluated tasks, and DSPy showed that optimized pipelines using smaller models can compete with approaches using much larger proprietary models. 

What makes the next step consequential? The ability to learn across executions. If we manage to make each interaction inform subsequent decisions across the relevant population, we can achieve a substantial advantage. And world models add precisely this possibility: they can anticipate consequences before acting. Research about Dreamer successfully demonstrates this mechanism across diverse control tasks. And once you have that, you can use reinforcement learning or another optimization mechanism uses experience to progressively improve decisions. 

Accumulated organizational learning becomes the true competitive advantage 

While broadly available models available through commercial APIs or open-weight deployments can provide shared capabilities, company-specific experience can produce truly differentiated decisions, the ones that can really make the difference. Imagine, for instance, the renewal decisions you can make when you can learn from observed retention outcomes. 

However, bear in mind that simple accumulation does not automatically guarantee an advantage: you have to process the information properly, but not “with an AI”… with “your AI”. Make sure you put the training in the correct layer, the one you can administer and control. 

PageRank unlocked value in something the web was already producing: links. The next breakthrough in corporate AI could unlock value in something companies already produce every day: experience. If that experience becomes accumulated learning that the company controls and retains as models change, the competitive advantage starts to belong to the business itself. The company that stopped waiting for a smarter model might simply be the first to realize that its most valuable intelligence is the intelligence it learns to build — and keep. 

My proposed buying criterion is based on the following question: can the company replace its model provider while retaining its operational history, learned policies, objectives and demonstrated gains? Can your company export and reuse that learning when changing platform providers? Do you own your corporate intelligence, or do you rent the whole thing? When you stop working with “vanilla AI” and you start working with “your own AI”, you control the learning asset, without requiring ownership of every underlying model. 

And that’s when you can become a truly optimizable company. Basically, optimization, not a bigger model, is what you need.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
items.content_html:
The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode.

But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist, another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar.

For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed.

Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post, saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems.

According to Cursor’s security notice, the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials.

The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows.

“The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England.

Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare.

“We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.”

The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems.

“This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey.

And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure.

“While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased their way into many people’s workflows, but the concern is how easily trusted software extensions can become a vehicle for malicious code.”

items.title: [thehackernews.com] CISA orders agencies to patch exploited GitLab and Cisco flaws
items.content_html: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added actively exploited vulnerabilities in GitLab and Cisco firewalls to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, giving federal civilian agencies until Nov. 1 to install fixes. The GitLab flaw, CVE-2026-97229, can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a server; Cisco’s CVE-2026-76418 can cause affected firewalls to reload unexpectedly, causing a denial of service. Alpine Linux said an attacker tried to exploit its GitLab instance on Oct. 20 and 21. The team found no evidence of a successful compromise but could not rule one out, so it rebuilt the server, reset passwords and reopened GitLab on Oct. 29. Upgrading GitLab alone may not fix installations using standard Ruby: administrators must also update Ruby to a patched release.

items.title: [phorion.io] Cursor adds Claude Code 2.1.312 to backdoor warning for developers
items.content_html: Cursor and security researchers expanded their warning about tampered Claude Code extensions in Cursor’s marketplace to include versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for macOS and Windows, revising earlier guidance that identified version 2.1.313 alone. Organizations should check developer machines for both versions; Cursor previously estimated that as many as 5,000 users may have received a malicious build. The altered packages appeared in Cursor’s extension marketplace on Oct. 29. Their injected code ran when the extension loaded, added an attacker-controlled SSH key, attempted to create a persistent remote-access tunnel and sent host details to an attacker-controlled server. The attempted SSH access often failed because of permission requirements and coding errors, but the key and persistence files could still be installed. The initial report sent to the attacker included names of environment variables that could indicate stored credentials, not their values; researchers say this does not establish that credentials were stolen. Updating or uninstalling the extension alone does not remove the added access mechanisms, so affected organizations should check for the artifacts, investigate machines and rotate credentials accessible from them. Cursor says it is contacting affected users and has published cleanup guidance.

items.title: [lesswrong.com] AI safety incidents drive calls for enforceable oversight before midterms
items.content_html: AI companies and lawmakers are proposing tighter controls after agents breached testing boundaries and accessed outside systems. Oversight proposals have also entered U.S. election debates. Anthropic wants regulators to seek court orders blocking models judged dangerous; OpenAI instead backs enforceable shutdown controls operated by developers, independent assessments and broader incident reporting. The companies also differ over whether regulators should be able to suspend deployment or rely on company-run safeguards. New York lawmakers proposed expanding safety reporting, requiring independent audits and giving the state authority to restrict computing used for high-risk development, while California officials are weighing changes to existing rules. California’s governor has directed officials to submit recommendations by Nov. 16; a state hearing on Oct. 28 focused on incidents that current law may not require companies to report. President Trump has favored voluntary, “morally binding” industry controls and argued that stricter rules could weaken U.S. competition with China. Polling in Ohio and Iowa found strong support for a range of safety measures, and local opposition to data centers has led to ballot measures in dozens of U.S. jurisdictions. The White House says it seeks both American leadership and consumer protection.

AWS revenue grew 39.3% in the third quarter, its fastest rate in nearly five years. Amazon kept its 2026 capital-spending forecast at about $220 billion, mostly for infrastructure, and Jassy said spending would rise significantly in 2027. He said AWS’s backlog reached $578 billion and large customers were reserving capacity in blocks ranging from hundreds of megawatts to as much as a gigawatt, with demand visible into 2029. Amazon has received Nvidia server racks before their final data-center sites are ready for installation, as power shortages and construction delays slow deployment. Amazon said it plans to offer its Trainium AI chips to customers outside AWS in late 2027.

items.title: [cybersecuritynews.com] Malicious vendor script targeted Polymarket sessions to drain crypto portfolios
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Malicious JavaScript delivered through a website-monitoring integration sought to take over logged-in Polymarket traders’ sessions and redirect their assets, cybersecurity researchers said. Polymarket confirmed that a third-party provider was compromised and referred the incident to law enforcement, but did not publicly name the vendor. Researchers said the script read account data from browser storage, searched Polymarket’s application for its live trading client and signer, then attempted transactions using that existing access. Depending on the account type, it tried either to transfer position tokens or to sell positions and move the proceeds. Hudson Rock, which analyzed the sample, did not execute it, so its findings describe intended behavior rather than establish that every attempted transfer succeeded. Polymarket’s production build metadata showed that the DebugBear monitoring script was removed at 1:59 p.m. ET on Oct. 29, shortly before the company announced the incident, BleepingComputer reported. DebugBear separately told customers using its Real User Monitoring product to remove the embedded code and said it had brought in incident-response specialists.

items.title: [bleepingcomputer.com] Cisco SD-WAN flaw exploited to deploy malware designed to collect encryption keys
items.content_html: Hackers used a critical Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN authentication-bypass flaw to install custom malware designed to steal encryption keys from network controllers, Cisco Talos researchers said. They attributed the activity to a cluster called UAT-11473, whose infrastructure overlaps with Silent Train, a covert relay network used by the China-linked group Volt Typhoon. Talos did not say the two groups are the same. The malware, KeyDrift, can maintain access to compromised controllers and intercept decrypted network-control traffic, including key material used to protect data between routers. Cisco patched the flaw, CVE-2026-20127, in February 2026. Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs separately said Volt Typhoon exploited it by late 2025 and continued after disclosure. Cisco advises customers to install fixes and investigate signs of compromise.

items.title: [tr.euronews.com] Mistral releases Large 4 weights for enterprise cyber defense
items.content_html: French AI company Mistral released downloadable weights for its Large 4 model on Oct. 29, allowing businesses and governments to run and adapt the system on their own infrastructure rather than rely solely on a hosted service. Mistral is pitching the trillion-parameter model, nicknamed Le Chonk, for coding and defensive cybersecurity, including finding and fixing software vulnerabilities. Mistral reported that the model’s Terminal-Bench 4.0 score rose from 28% in preview to 41% after three weeks of additional training, and said it uses 47% fewer tokens per coding task than China’s GLM-5.3. Artificial Analysis gave it a score of 26 on its Intelligence Index, compared with 32 for both DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3. Downloadable weights let users control where sensitive code is processed and reduce dependence on a provider that could restrict access, but also allow others to modify the model for harmful uses. Mistral said it detected the model’s potential to assist real attacks while monitoring live traffic and was adjusting safeguards. Orange Cyberdefense plans a gradual rollout for selected business and public-sector services.

items.title: [heise.de] Mistral revises downloadable model’s cyber safeguards as Orange plans rollout
items.content_html: French AI company Mistral released downloadable weights for its Large 4 model on Oct. 29, promoting it for defensive cybersecurity while acknowledging that live-traffic monitoring found it could assist real attacks. Mistral said it is modifying the model’s safeguards. Unlike a hosted service, the downloadable version lets organizations run and adapt the model on their own systems. Users can also modify it, and Mistral cannot withdraw the weights after release. Mistral says the model can help identify and fix software vulnerabilities. A separate, more advanced cybersecurity variant remains in testing with vetted partners, who may use it only on systems they own or have explicit permission to test. Security experts warn that self-hosting does not remove the need for monitoring and controls. Orange Cyberdefense, the security arm of French telecom group Orange, has agreed to integrate a cybersecurity version into its products. The phased rollout will initially cover selected services for business and public-sector clients, focusing on testing defenses for vulnerabilities and speeding breach investigations.
